series_items.subject: [PATCH 01/22] mm: add node-state-filtered zone and node iterators
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds helper functions and macros to the Linux kernel's memory management (mm) subsystem, allowing MM walkers to select node eligibility explicitly. It introduces nodemask intersection and nodemask/state iterators using bitmap intersection helpers without allocating temporary nodemasks. The patch includes new macros for iterating over zones on nodes in a specific state, enabling more efficient and targeted memory allocation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 02/22] mm: publish and clear node memory states via helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch centralizes the updates of node memory states by introducing two new functions, `node_set_memory_state` and `node_clear_memory_state`, which replace the separate calls to set and clear individual state flags in various places throughout the code. The behavior remains unchanged, but the code is simplified and easier to maintain. The patch also removes redundant checks for high and normal memory states, making it more efficient.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 03/22] mm: introduce the common-memory node state
series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces the concept of 'common memory' in Linux, which refers to memory that can be managed by the kernel's MM services without needing explicit node requests. It adds a new node state called N_MEMORY_COMMON and exposes this information through sysfs attributes. The patch also updates documentation and APIs to reflect these changes, allowing userspace to identify nodes with common memory available for ordinary allocations.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 04/22] mm/page_alloc: build zonelists from common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the way zonelists are built in the Linux kernel's memory management system. Instead of building fallback lists for all nodes and local lists only for non-common nodes, it builds common memory zonelists from N_MEMORY_COMMON and local-only zonelists for common nodes. This change is achieved by refactoring the build_local_zonelist function to reuse code for building a local-only zonelist for nodes outside the common set. The patch does not affect nodes with no memory, as they do not have zones to list anyway.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 05/22] mm/mempolicy: keep interleave and tmpfs mount policies on common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's memory policy to use a new set of common memory nodes (N_MEMORY_COMMON) instead of N_MEMORY for boot memory policy calculations and their per-node sysfs entries. It also restricts the node set applied by mpol_set_nodemask() and mbind() masks to N_MEMORY_COMMON nodes. This change is intended to simplify the management of memory policies and ensure that all memory is considered common at this point, with no immediate behavior changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 06/22] mm: base hash distribution on common memory nodes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the hash distribution mechanism to base its decisions on common memory nodes, rather than all memory nodes. This change is made by counting the number of common memory nodes when applying a single-node optimization. As all memory is currently considered common, the behavior remains unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 07/22] mm/memory_hotplug: migrate offlined pages to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the memory hotplug migration code to restrict the destination nodes for page migration to only those that are marked as N_MEMORY_COMMON. This change prevents the destination nodemask from becoming empty when migrating pages to a node that is not an eligible allocation target, which can occur in certain configurations where some nodes are marked as N_MEMORY but not N_MEMORY_COMMON.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 08/22] mm/memory-tiers: restrict demotion topology to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the demotion topology in Linux's memory-tiers to only consider common memory (N_MEMORY_COMMON). It achieves this by modifying several functions that build demotion paths and assign nodes to memory tiers, ensuring that these operations are limited to nodes within N_MEMORY_COMMON. This change does not affect existing behavior for nodes carrying N_MEMORY_COMMON, as all current nodes do so. The patch aims to improve the management of memory allocation and demotion in the Linux kernel by reducing unnecessary complexity and potential issues related to non-common memory nodes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 09/22] mm/ksm: restrict merging to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the merging of memory pages to only common memory, excluding ZONE_DEVICE folios and non-anonymous memory. The change is made in two locations where KSM (Kernel Samepage Merging) service acquires memory pages. This ensures that KSM does not attempt to merge memory outside the ordinary memory pool, which aligns with its opportunistic nature.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 10/22] mm/khugepaged: restrict collapse to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the collapse operation in the mm/khugepaged module to only common memory, which is memory that can be shared between processes. The existing checks for zone device pages are replaced with a check for common memory using the page_is_common_memory() function. Additionally, a new check is added to the collapse_scan_file() function to ensure that page-cache folios are also restricted to common memory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 11/22] mm/mempolicy: don't NUMA-hint folios outside common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the NUMA balancing scanner to not inject hint faults or migrate folios that are outside of common memory, which includes zone device memory. The existing check for zone device memory is replaced with a more general check for common memory. As all memory is considered common at this point, the behavior remains unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 12/22] mm/damon: restrict DAMON-native folio operations to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts DAMON-native folio operations to common memory, preventing them from being performed on memory outside of N_MEMORY_COMMON. This change treats these folios like ZONE_DEVICE memory and prevents DAMON from acquiring or aging them. As a result, virtual address monitoring will report accessed pages as such, and migration is restricted to destinations within N_MEMORY_COMMON.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 13/22] mm/hugetlb: restrict pool growth to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the growth of HugeTLB pools to nodes that have common memory, preventing allocations on nodes without this capability. The change is made by modifying various functions in the mm/hugetlb.c file to use N_MEMORY_COMMON instead of N_MEMORY for allocating and growing hugepage pools. This restriction can be loosened later if needed. Currently, all memory is considered common, so the behavior remains unchanged.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 14/22] mm/page_alloc: count common memory nodes for kswapd recovery
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the behavior of free_frozen_page_commit() to only clear kswapd hopeless state when there is more than one common memory node, rather than any memory node. This change ensures that direct reclaim is triggered even if allocations fall back to another node without triggering it initially. The patch does not alter behavior since all memory is considered common at this point.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 15/22] mm/oom_kill: compare OOM constraints against common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the OOM (Out of Memory) killer's behavior to compare policy and cpuset constraints against common memory, rather than all memory. This change ensures that nodes outside the common memory zone do not artificially inflate the constrained capacity or make global policies appear constrained. The modification is made in the mm/oom_kill.c file and does not affect behavior when all memory is considered common.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 16/22] tty/sysrq: use common memory for the manual OOM zonelist
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the manual OOM (Out-Of-Memory) zonelist in the sysrq driver to use common memory instead of every node that has memory. This change ensures that the fallback domain for ordinary allocations contains only common memory, which is a more accurate representation of the system's available resources. The behavior remains unchanged because all nodes are considered common at this point.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 17/22] mm/vmscan: restrict reclaim to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the reclaim process to common memory, which is a type of memory that can be shared among multiple nodes in a system. The changes include starting kswapd only on common nodes at boot or hotplug time, walking only common zones during direct reclaim and throttling, and using common nodes when MGLRU registers an mm or iterates/validates nodes. This approach ensures that the reclaim process is more efficient and effective by focusing on memory that can be easily shared and reclaimed.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 18/22] mm/compaction: restrict compaction to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the compaction process in Linux to common memory only, which is a subset of all available memory. The changes include modifying the kcompactd daemon to start on common nodes at boot and hotplug, limiting direct compaction to common zones, and restricting proactive compaction to common nodes. This approach aims to improve system performance by focusing compaction efforts on areas where it will have the most impact.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 19/22] mm/migrate: restrict move_pages() destinations to common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch restricts the destination of the move_pages() function to common memory, rejecting any node without common memory. This change aligns with how memory policies work and ensures that user memory is placed on a general-purpose node. Currently, all memory is considered common, so this patch does not introduce any behavioral changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 20/22] PM: hibernate: size the image from common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the hibernation image size calculation to only count free pages in zones on nodes that are marked as common memory, rather than all populated zones. This ensures that the hibernation image can be stored in common memory. The patch also separates the image metadata estimate from the page frame tracking, which is still calculated for all populated zones.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 21/22] mm/khugepaged: base the recommended min_free_kbytes on common memory
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adjusts the calculation for recommended min_free_kbytes in the khugepaged module to reserve memory only on nodes that are marked as N_MEMORY_COMMON, which represents common memory. This change helps THP allocations avoid fragmentation by reserving two pageblocks per populated zone on these nodes. The recommendation remains unchanged for all other nodes with memory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 22/22] nodemask: remove the now-unused first_memory_node/next_memory_node
series_items.patch_summary: This patch removes two unused helper functions, first_memory_node and next_memory_node, from the Linux kernel's nodemask code. These functions were previously used to get the first or next node in a specific state, but their usage has been replaced by explicit naming of the desired state. The removal of these helpers forces new code to explicitly choose a node state instead of silently defaulting to N_MEMORY.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series introduces N_MEMORY_COMMON, a new concept for general-purpose memory separate from node memory (N_MEMORY). It creates a baseline to ensure private node memory is default opted-out of being touched by the MM, similar to ZONE_DEVICE. The series consists of three phases: introducing N_MEMORY_COMMON, defining memory not part of the general pool (N_MEMORY_PRIVATE), and adding feature bits for userland management.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 1/4] mm: zswap: fix shrinker count for the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the zswap shrinker that incorrectly calculates the number of freeable entries for the root memory cgroup (memcg). The issue arises from the fact that the root memcg's stats do not account for its own zswap entries, leading to incorrect scaling and failure to reclaim pages. To fix this, the patch uses the zswap pool-wide counters instead of the memcg's statistics for the root memcg. This change ensures accurate calculation of freeable entries and enables proper page reclamation.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 2/4] mm: memcg: read root lruvec stats from the node counters
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the root memory cgroup's (memcg) LRU vector stats are read by using the node counters instead of flushing the entire system when possible. This is done for most memcg node stats, which only track memory charged to a memcg, and the root memcg's hierarchical value equals the node counter. However, certain kernel memory stats, hugetlb, and WORKINGSET_NODERECLAIM still require reading the rstat value due to accounting complexities. The patch also updates the way these stats are reported in the cgroup v1 memory.numa_stat, making it more accurate but potentially mismatching with the root memcg's memory.stat.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 3/4] mm: workingset: skip the root memcg flush in workingset_test_recent()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the workingset_test_recent() function by skipping the root memory cgroup (memcg) flush when it's not necessary. The function now checks if the eviction memcg is the root memcg, and if so, reads the LRU sizes directly from the node counters instead of flushing the stats. This reduces the overhead of a root flush from 69us to ~150ns on an 80-CPU machine with little cgroup activity. The patch also keeps the flush for reclaim operations as it's still needed to keep up-to-date statistics.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v3 4/4] mm/damon/core: use node counters instead of flushing the root memcg
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the damos_get_node_memcg_used_bp function to use node counters instead of flushing the root memcg's statistics when calculating LRU sizes. This change improves performance by avoiding unnecessary flushes and leveraging up-to-date node counter data for the root cgroup.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series modifies how memory cgroup (memcg) statistics are read from the root cgroup, which is a critical component in Linux's memory management system. Currently, reading memcg stats for the root cgroup involves flushing all other cgroups' stats, which can be expensive and introduce latency. This patch proposes to instead use global counters that track memory usage across all cgroups, eliminating the need for these flushes. The changes are incremental, with some call sites already using global counters, while others will require additional patches to adapt. The goal is to reduce overhead and improve performance in scenarios where the root cgroup's stats are accessed frequently.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Linux kernel's compaction algorithm to sample empty pageblocks from a random offset when the initial scan finds nothing. This is done to prevent aliasing issues that can cause free pages to be missed, particularly in sparse layouts or when memory is not aligned with the sampling grid. The change aims to improve the detection of free pages and reduce the likelihood of compaction failures, which can lead to stalled tasks and inefficient memory usage.

That is where it gets hairy: will this be observable in real workloads?

Suppose stride is 32 and the pageblock has 100 non-free pages. What is
the probability that 512 slots are filled with 100 objects such that
x = 0 (mod 32) is filled? It is

C(496, 84) / C(512, 100) = 1.6 *10^(-12), very improbable.

So the chance you have a sparse block and you are missing out by not
looking at other offsets is very low.

If stride = 32 and #objects = 400, the probability comes out to be
1.8%.

Keeping #objects fixed, lowering the stride lowers the probability
exponentially. (This is relevant since we start with lower strides)

On the other hand, what happens if you are scanning over fully filled
memory? (there is no way to tell whether a pageblock is sparse)
You are going to repeat the scans unnecessarily.

IOW I think the probability this patch is going to have a downside is
more than that of upside.

series_items.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new mutex, cgroup_bpf_mutex, to protect the BPF state in cgroups. Only attach, detach, and replace operations require both cgroup_mutex and cgroup_bpf_mutex, while other operations like query, link info, and release work only need cgroup_bpf_mutex. This change is motivated by performance issues in a Meta fleet where tasks waiting for cgroup_mutex were experiencing long delays.

review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Linus Torvalds pointed out that many memcpy() calls are not actual function calls on a C level and that the compiler should be relied upon to optimize small memcpy() calls into loads and stores, making it inefficient to hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for performance reasons.
review_comments.raw_body:
The problem with this approach two-fold:

 - many memcpy() calls aren't actually memcpy() calls on a C level

 - many memcpy() that *are* calls on a C level should never be calls
in the generated code

That first case is for things like structure copies etc. And it's
common, and it's important, although for the kernel it's usually a
non-issue because it's *typicay* a small constant-sized copy, which
brings us to the second case...

The second case is hugely important. The compiler needs to turn small
memcpy() calls into just loads and stores. Calling "memcpy()" for a
known 64-byte copy is hugely inefficient.

We used to - long ago - do that "constant small sizes" thing by hand.
It was a huge pain. We now rely on the compiler to do it.

End result: we must *not* hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for
performance reasons, and we cannot catch all cases anyway because the
compiler generates implicit memcpy calls.

This is why I really wish we had the compiler just generate a
different sequence for 'call memcpy'. One that used a different
callign convention - preferably just the 'rep movs' one so that we
could just rewrite the call with 'rep movsb' in place.

Without compiler support, we're kind of screwed.

              Linus

review_comments.author: Linus Torvalds
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that many memcpy() calls are not actual function calls and that the compiler should be relied upon to optimize small copies into loads and stores, rather than hiding 'memcpy()' from it for performance reasons.
review_comments.raw_body:
The problem with this approach two-fold:

 - many memcpy() calls aren't actually memcpy() calls on a C level

 - many memcpy() that *are* calls on a C level should never be calls
in the generated code

That first case is for things like structure copies etc. And it's
common, and it's important, although for the kernel it's usually a
non-issue because it's *typicay* a small constant-sized copy, which
brings us to the second case...

The second case is hugely important. The compiler needs to turn small
memcpy() calls into just loads and stores. Calling "memcpy()" for a
known 64-byte copy is hugely inefficient.

We used to - long ago - do that "constant small sizes" thing by hand.
It was a huge pain. We now rely on the compiler to do it.

End result: we must *not* hide 'memcpy()' from the compiler for
performance reasons, and we cannot catch all cases anyway because the
compiler generates implicit memcpy calls.

This is why I really wish we had the compiler just generate a
different sequence for 'call memcpy'. One that used a different
callign convention - preferably just the 'rep movs' one so that we
could just rewrite the call with 'rep movsb' in place.

Without compiler support, we're kind of screwed.

              Linus
